units.title: Unit 01 — The family
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 1, textbook pp. 8–9 (PDF pp. 9–10); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: There are five people in our family.
items.note: In British English, family may have two or three syllables: /ˈfæmli/ or /ˈfæməli/.

items.example: We drew a family tree with three generations.
items.note: Use a family-tree diagram to work out relationships between different relatives.

items.example: Some of my relatives live abroad.
items.note: Relatives and relations can both mean family members; they are not limited to the immediate family.

items.example: She invited several relations to the celebration.
items.note: In this context, relations means relatives. Relation also has other meanings in different contexts.

items.example: Her husband works in a nearby town.
His wife is a musician.
items.note: Irregular plural: wife → wives /waɪvz/, not wifes.

items.example: Both men introduced their wives.
items.note: Compare wife /waɪf/ and wives /waɪvz/: the final consonant changes from /f/ to /v/.

items.example: My father enjoys cooking.
items.note: The /ð/ sound is voiced, as in mother.

items.example: My mother called me yesterday.
Both parents attended the meeting.
items.note: Parents refers to two or more parents; use parent for one mother, father, or other parent.

items.example: Each parent signed the form.
items.note: The singular form of parents. This is a teaching extension to practise parent versus parents.

items.example: They have one son.
Their daughter is learning to swim.
items.note: In British English, the letters gh are silent in daughter.

items.example: The children are playing in the garden.
items.note: The irregular plural of child is children, not childs.

items.example: Their youngest child is seven years old.
items.note: Irregular plural: children. Child does not specify gender.

items.example: My sister is older than me.
Her brother studies in London.
items.note: Use possessive ’s to express a relationship: Julia’s brother is Julia’s male sibling.

items.example: My grandfather tells wonderful stories.
His grandmother grows vegetables.
We visited our grandparents on Sunday.
items.note: Grandparents refers collectively to grandmothers and grandfathers.

items.example: Their granddaughter started school today.
His grandson loves football.
My uncle lives by the sea.
Her aunt teaches mathematics.
items.note: British pronunciation: /ɑːnt/. The pronunciation /ænt/ is common in American English.

items.example: I bought a book for my niece.
items.note: A niece is the daughter of your brother or sister (and can also be related by marriage).

items.example: My nephew is ten years old.
My cousin is coming to stay this weekend.
items.note: Cousin can refer to a male or female cousin.

items.example: I am an only child, so I have no brothers or sisters.
items.note: Only son does not necessarily mean only child; the person may have sisters.

items.example: She comes from a big family.
My colleague comes from a big family.
items.note: A common question about family size is: Do you come from a big family?

items.example: Do you have any brothers and sisters?
items.note: In informal British English, you may also ask: Have you got any brothers and sisters?

items.pt: ter; possuir (uso comum no inglês britânico)
items.example: I have got two brothers.
items.note: Have you got…? and Do you have…? can both express possession. Do not confuse this with the past tense of get.

learningObjectives: Identify family relationships in a family tree, including from another person's point of view.
Use singular and plural family vocabulary and understand relatives and relations.
Ask about siblings, cousins, and large families; explain when someone is an only child.
Distinguish wife and wives and use possessive forms to describe family relationships.
Write and describe a family tree in English.

units.title: Unit 02 — Birth, marriage and death
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 2, textbook pp. 10–11 (PDF pp. 11–12); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: The baby slept for most of the afternoon.

items.pt: ter um bebê; dar à luz
items.example: My neighbour had a baby last month.
items.note: Use had a baby to describe a birth, not got a baby.

items.example: My brother was born in 2002.
items.note: Use was born or were born to talk about birth in the past. Do not say He born.

items.example: The newborn baby weighs just over three kilograms.
items.note: The present-tense form is weighs; the past tense is weighed. The letters gh are silent.

items.example: The baby weighed four kilograms at birth.
items.note: The simple past of weigh; pronounced /weɪd/.

items.pt: dar a alguém o nome de outra pessoa; homenagear no nome
items.example: They called their daughter Rosa after her grandmother.
items.note: Here, after identifies the person whose name inspired the choice; name someone after is also possible.

items.example: My birthday is on the ninth of April.
items.note: Use on with an exact date and in with a year: born on 9 April; born in 2002.

items.example: The family celebrated the birth of their daughter.
items.note: Birth is a noun; born is a past participle used in the expression be born.

items.example: My aunt was born in 1970.
items.note: Use in with a year, month, or city: born in 1970; born in London.

items.example: The child was born on a Monday.
items.note: Use on with a day or date: born on Monday; born on 12 June.

items.example: The baby was born at half past seven in the morning.
items.note: Use at for a time, on for a day or date, and in for a month, year, or place: born at 7:30; born on Monday; born in March.

items.example: Her partner came to the party.
items.note: Partner can describe a romantic relationship without specifying marital status or gender.

items.example: He is single at the moment.
items.note: In this context, single describes relationship status.

items.example: They are married and live near the station.
items.note: Be married describes marital status; get married describes the act of marrying.

items.example: She was widowed when her husband died.
items.note: Widowed means that a spouse has died; it is different from divorced.

items.example: They are separated but have not divorced.
items.note: Separated does not necessarily mean that the divorce has been finalized.

items.example: My uncle has been divorced for five years.
items.note: Divorced refers to the legal dissolution of a marriage.

items.example: Their marriage lasted twelve years.
items.note: Marriage refers to the relationship or institution; wedding refers to the ceremony or celebration.

items.example: The couple decided to break up.
items.note: When a marriage breaks up, the couple stops living together as a couple.

items.example: The wedding took place on Saturday.
items.note: A wedding is the ceremony or celebration; marriage can refer to the ongoing relationship.

items.example: The bride arrived with her family.
items.note: On the wedding day, the bride is the woman getting married.

items.example: The groom was waiting outside the church.
items.note: Groom is a shorter form of bridegroom.

items.example: My friends got married last summer.
items.note: Get married describes the act of marrying; be married describes marital status. They married in 2001 is also possible and is more formal.

items.example: She got married to her long-time partner.
items.note: Say married to someone, not married with someone.

items.example: They were married for twenty years.
items.note: Use for to express duration: married for ten years.

items.example: They spent their honeymoon in Greece.

items.pt: ir passar a lua de mel
items.example: The couple went on honeymoon after the wedding.
items.note: Say on honeymoon, not in honeymoon.

items.example: He became ill during the trip.
Some insects die after only a few days.
items.note: Die is a verb; dead is an adjective; death is a noun.

items.example: The scientist died many years ago.
items.note: Died is the past tense of die. To describe a state, use is dead, not is died.

items.example: His grandfather died of pneumonia.
items.note: Die of is used with many causes of death, including illnesses and old age.

items.example: The patient survived a heart attack.
items.note: Say have a heart attack; do not use get a heart attack in this meaning.

items.example: The old tree is dead.
items.note: Dead is an adjective: is dead. Do not confuse it with died, the past tense of die.

items.example: The family heard about his death yesterday.
items.note: Death is a noun; die is a verb; dead is an adjective.

items.example: Friends and relatives attended the funeral.

learningObjectives: Talk about birth using have a baby, be born, weigh, dates, and naming someone after another person.
Distinguish single, married, widowed, separated, and divorced.
Identify bride, groom, wedding, honeymoon, and marriage-related prepositions.
Distinguish die, died, dead, death, and funeral in context.
Avoid common errors: had a baby (not got a baby), was born, and married to (not married with).
Create original sentences about birth, marriage, and life events.
Use at for birth times, on for days and dates, and in for months, years, and places.
